questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Qualitative versus quantitative research question
questions.learningObjective: match a research question to the design that can answer it
questions.stem: A team has decided to study a new starter's first month in a hospital ward qualitatively. Which research question can that design actually answer?

options.text: How do new joiners learn the unwritten rules that keep the team working?
Does induction cut time to first task by thirty percent, as the trust requires?
options.misconception: assumes any workplace question suits a qualitative design once the label is chosen

options.text: How many new joiners manage their first task within their first week?
options.misconception: calls a bare count a qualitative question because the topic is people rather than numbers

options.text: Is this year's new joiner turnover rate higher than the previous year was?
options.misconception: mistakes a comparison between two rates for a question about how people experience the work

questions.explanation: A qualitative design earns its keep on questions about process, meaning and language, and only option A asks how something is learned and done. The design choice constrains the question rather than following it, so a percentage target or a headcount belongs to a quantitative design that could report an estimate, and the trap is assuming that because the subject is human the qualitative label fits any wording at all.
questions.hint: Ask which question needs the participants' own words in the answer.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Positivist and constructivist epistemologies
questions.learningObjective: identify the claim about reality that underlies each research stance
questions.stem: Two teams disagree about what counts as evidence. Which pairing correctly attaches each stance to the claim it makes about reality?

options.text: Positivism: an objective reality exists and constructivism: meaning is made, not found
Positivism: meaning is made, not found and constructivism: an objective reality exists
options.misconception: swaps the two positions, treating the stances as interchangeable labels

options.text: Positivism: only large samples count and constructivism: only interviews count
options.misconception: reduces each stance to a preferred method rather than a claim about reality

options.text: Positivism: the researcher must stay neutral and constructivism: the researcher must argue
options.misconception: confuses a stance about reality with the researcher's style or temperament

questions.explanation: Positivism holds that a reality exists independently of the researcher and can be measured, which is what licenses estimating a quantity and testing it against a rival account. Constructivism holds that the object of study is meaning as it is produced, so the work is to elicit and analyse that meaning rather than to measure a fixed thing, and confusing the two is what makes a team argue about sample size when it should be arguing about what counts as knowing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the stance treats the object as a thing or as a meaning.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: How a grounded theory's theory emerges
questions.learningObjective: explain why a grounded theory cannot be read off a prior framework
questions.stem: A team publishes a study billed as grounded theory. Which feature of the finished work shows the theory grew out of the data rather than being imported?

options.text: The categories were built and revised against the material, with early versions shown to differ from the final one
The paper cites the framework the authors say the data were read through
options.misconception: treats a cited framework as evidence that the categories came from the data

options.text: The interviews were long enough that every participant said something interesting
options.misconception: equates interview length with the theory having emerged from the analysis

options.text: The write-up uses the word grounded theory in its title and its abstract
options.misconception: reads a label in the title as a description of how the analysis proceeded

questions.explanation: Grounded theory earns its name only if the categories are accountable to the material, so a revision trail in which early codes differ from final ones is the evidence that they were not fixed in advance. A cited framework records the lens the authors brought, not the source of the categories, and a title is a promise rather than a method, so citing the framework or naming the approach cannot substitute for showing the analysis changed under contact with the data.
questions.hint: Look for evidence that the coding changed as the data were read.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What makes a case worth studying
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a case is analytically rather than merely conveniently chosen
questions.stem: A researcher can study any one hospital trust in the country. Which choice of trust is the strongest case selection for the question being asked?

options.text: The trust that first refused the new triage rule, so the disruption it caused can be examined closely
The trust nearest the university, because travel costs less for the interviewer each week
options.misconception: treats physical convenience to the researcher as a warrant for the case

options.text: The trust with the fewest complaints, because a calm site gives a clean picture of daily work
options.misconception: assumes a typical or quiet site is analytically informative about a disruption

options.text: The trust with the largest budget, because a large site can supply enough participants for the study
options.misconception: borrows the logic of quantitative sample size for a single case design

questions.explanation: A case earns its place by being analytically revealing for the question asked, and a trust that refused the rule is where the interesting consequences are most likely to be visible and concentrated. Convenience, quietness and size are all properties that feel like prudence but answer a different question, and the trap is that a large or well-run site sounds rigorous, when in a single case design what matters is that the case can show the process at work.
questions.hint: Ask which site would make the phenomenon hardest to miss.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The researcher's position in an ethnography
questions.learningObjective: identify the access and role an ethnographer must make explicit
questions.stem: A researcher spends four months in a warehouse and publishes it as ethnography. Which part of the write-up carries the weight of the method?

options.text: An account of how the researcher gained access and what their presence in the setting could and could not change
A statement that the researcher was present for the same number of hours as the least experienced worker
options.misconception: treats matching shift length as the whole account of a researcher's position

options.text: A list of every conversation held, so readers can count how much material was gathered
options.misconception: substitutes a count of contacts for an account of what access did to the setting

options.text: An assurance that the researcher took no notes during the first month, to stay out of the way
options.misconception: reads abstaining from note-taking as proof the researcher was uninfluential

questions.explanation: An ethnography is produced by a person who was there, so the access negotiated and the presence itself are part of the evidence, not a preface to it, and a reader needs both to judge what the account can carry. Matching hours, counting conversations and avoiding note-taking all describe logistics, and the trap is that they sound like rigour because they are countable, while the part that actually shapes the data is how the researcher was received and what the group did because of them.
questions.hint: Ask what the researcher's own presence did to the place.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What phenomenology brackets
questions.learningObjective: state what a phenomenological reduction sets aside and what it preserves
questions.stem: A phenomenologist describes the experience of waiting for a scan result. What does bracketing set aside in this work, and what does it leave in place?

options.text: It sets aside the researcher's own prior assumptions about waiting and keeps the described experience itself
It sets aside the participants' reported experience and keeps the researcher's interpretation of it
options.misconception: removes the phenomenon itself rather than the researcher's assumptions about it

options.text: It sets aside everything unique to each case and keeps only what every participant had in common
options.misconception: confuses bracketing with averaging away the variation between individual experiences

options.text: It sets aside the ethical approval and the consent forms and keeps the interview material intact
options.misconception: reads an intellectual discipline as though it were an administrative waiver

questions.explanation: Bracketing is a discipline on the researcher's own commitments, holding them in view and setting them aside for the duration of the description so the phenomenon can be described rather than read through them, and the experience under study is exactly what stays. Removing the participants' experience would leave nothing to describe, averaging the cases would erase the variation the method exists to capture, and the administrative reading confuses an intellectual move with the paperwork that surrounds a study.
questions.hint: Ask whose assumption is the thing being set aside.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Unit of analysis in content analysis
questions.learningObjective: state what a content analysis counts when the unit is fixed
questions.stem: A content analysis covers 240 news articles, each coded for up to three themes. What is the unit of analysis, and what does the count describe?

options.text: The article, so a count describes articles or the themes found within them
The theme, so a count describes how many articles a single theme reaches
options.misconception: counts the coding category as the unit and silently changes what the numbers mean

options.text: The sentence, so a count describes every clause in which a theme appears at all
options.misconception: assumes the finest text unit is the analytic unit without the codebook saying so

options.text: The author, so a count describes how often each writer returns to a theme
options.misconception: reassigns the unit to the source and reports a different denominator than the sample

questions.explanation: The unit of analysis is the thing a record stands for, and here a record is an article, so a count of themed articles describes how many items carry a theme, not how many themes exist in the abstract. The trap is that a codebook lists themes prominently, so the theme feels like the unit, but swapping it changes the denominator and every figure reported, and the same care is needed to keep the article from quietly becoming a sentence or a byline.
questions.hint: Ask what one row of the dataset represents.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Codebook versus emergent coding in thematic analysis
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a codebook-driven analysis from one that lets the code list grow
questions.stem: A team argues about how themes should be found. Which statement correctly separates a codebook-driven analysis from an emergent one?

options.text: A codebook fixes categories before coding starts, while an emergent one builds and revises them as the material is read
A codebook is written after coding, while an emergent one is written before the interviews begin
options.misconception: reverses the timing of the code list in each approach

options.text: A codebook is shared publicly, while an emergent one is kept inside the analysis team's own files
options.misconception: treats openness of the code list as the defining difference between the approaches

options.text: A codebook uses only interview data, while an emergent one draws on survey and diary material as well
options.misconception: confuses the two approaches with the kind of source material admitted

questions.explanation: What separates the approaches is when the category list is settled, not who may read it or what data it draws on, so a pre-specified codebook tests the material against categories chosen in advance while an emergent list is answerable to what the material keeps producing. The trap is that both are often shared and both can use the same sources, which makes the visibility and the data type look like the difference when the timing of the commitment is the real one.
questions.hint: Ask at what moment the category list stops changing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Deductive and inductive codes
questions.learningObjective: tell an anticipated code from one the material required
questions.stem: A researcher codes a transcript and finds a passage about a nurse rewriting a chart entry at night. Which reading of that code is deductive, and which is inductive?

options.text: Deductive if the code came from a pre-set list, inductive if the wording was taken from the participant
Deductive if the code is broad, inductive if the code is narrow and specific to the case
options.misconception: confuses the breadth of a code with where its justification comes from

options.text: Deductive if two coders agreed on it, inductive if only one coder applied it to the passage
options.misconception: reads agreement between coders as the source of a code's justification

options.text: Deductive if the passage supports the project's theory, inductive if it challenges the theory
options.misconception: makes agreement with a prior theory the test for whether a code is deductive

questions.explanation: Deductive and inductive describe where a code's warrant comes from, a pre-set list or the language of the material, and nothing about how wide the code is or how many coders agreed on it settles that. The trap is that a theory-consistent code feels deductive because the theory feels prior, but a code can be deductive with no theory in the design at all, and inductive codes are frequently broad rather than narrow.
questions.hint: Ask whether the code was expected before the passage was read.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement between coders
questions.learningObjective: compute a chance-corrected agreement coefficient from a coding table
questions.stem: Two coders each label fifty interview extracts for one theme. They assign the same label on forty-five extracts. Coder one calls thirty extracts present and coder two calls twenty-five. What is the chance-corrected agreement coefficient? Give the value to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Observed agreement is 45 over 50, which is 0.90, and the agreement two coders would reach by luck alone comes from their separate rates: 0.60 times 0.50 that both call an extract present, plus 0.40 times 0.50 that both call it absent, giving 0.50. The coefficient is the observed share minus the chance share, divided by what is left above chance, so 0.90 minus 0.50 over 1 minus 0.50 gives 0.80. The raw 0.90 flatters the coders because two of them working from the same material would agree on plenty of extracts for no better reason than a coin landing the same way twice.
questions.hint: Find the agreement the two coders would hit by chance, then correct the observed share against it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Discarding singleton codes
questions.learningObjective: compute the surviving code count after singleton codes are folded in
questions.stem: A study begins with six codes fixed in advance. Across fifteen interviews eleven further codes are named, of which four are applied in only one interview each and get folded into existing codes. How many codes survive?
questions.explanation: The six pre-set codes all remain, and of the eleven codes that arose only the seven used in more than one interview are kept, so six plus seven is thirteen. The four singletons are dropped because a category that appears once is usually this participant's own wording rather than a pattern the sample shares, and the trap is counting all eleven arrivals as new findings when the point of merging them is to stop a single voice becoming a category.

questions.topic: How widespread a theme is across interviews
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of interviews in which a theme appears
questions.stem: A thematic analysis of sixteen interviews finds one theme present in eleven of them. What proportion of the interviews carry that theme? Give the value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The share is the number of interviews carrying the theme over the number interviewed, so eleven over sixteen is 0.6875, a little under seven in ten. The trap is dividing by the number of coded passages instead, which makes a theme look ubiquitous because a single long interview contributes many passages, and the denominator has to be the people or cases that were studied, not the fragments the coder happened to mark.

questions.topic: Share of talk time in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: compute one participant's share of total group talk time
questions.stem: A focus group of eight runs for fifty-two minutes. A talk-time log shows one participant speaking for twenty-one minutes with the other seven sharing the rest. What share of the total talk time did that participant take? Give the value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Share of talk time is the participant's minutes over the group's total, so twenty-one over fifty-two is 0.4038, just over two fifths of the airtime, which is well above the one eighth an even distribution would give. The trap is dividing by the seven other participants or by the remaining thirty-one minutes, both of which answer a different question, and the figure matters because a dominated discussion understates the views of everyone who stayed quiet.

questions.topic: Unequal sample sizes across mixed phases
questions.learningObjective: compare the sizes of a qualitative and a quantitative phase
questions.stem: An exploratory sequential design interviews twenty people in its first phase and then recruits six hundred survey respondents in its second. By what factor is the second sample larger than the first?
questions.explanation: The factor is the second sample over the first, so six hundred over twenty is thirty, and the two phases are not expected to match because the survey is sized to estimate with precision while the interviews are sized to find out what is worth asking. questions.topic: Extracts with no majority code
questions.learningObjective: count the units that three coders cannot settle between them
questions.stem: Three coders each classify sixty extracts. On forty-two all three assign the same code, on thirteen exactly two agree and one dissents, and on five all three assign different codes. How many extracts have no majority code and need a decision before analysis?
questions.explanation: An extract is settled when at least two coders chose the same code, so the forty-two unanimous and the thirteen with a two-to-one split are both decided, leaving only the five where all three differ. Those five are the ones that must go to adjudication or a codebook clarification, and the trap is counting the thirteen as unresolved too, which treats a working majority as though a tie-breaking vote had not settled the question.

questions.topic: New codes per interview after the plateau
questions.learningObjective: compute the rate of new codes in the interviews that follow the plateau
questions.stem: A team codes twenty-four interviews in order. New codes appear in the first nine. The fifteen interviews from the tenth onwards add no new code at all. What is the average number of new codes per interview across those fifteen?

questions.topic: Coverage of a joint display
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of findings that are actually integrated in a joint display
questions.stem: A mixed study reports nine qualitative findings and six quantitative results. Its joint display places seven of those items in paired rows, leaving two findings and one result unpaired. What share of all fifteen items appears in a paired row?

questions.topic: Counting theme instances at the unit of analysis
questions.learningObjective: count coded instances from a stated unit and an instance ceiling
questions.stem: A content analysis takes 240 articles as its unit and allows up to three coded themes per article. Forty-five articles contain no codeable theme at all. How many coded theme instances does the analysis produce?
questions.explanation: Only the articles that carry a code contribute, so the 195 coded articles at up to three themes each give 585 instances, and the ceiling means this is a maximum rather than a guaranteed count. The trap is multiplying all 240 by three, which silently invents 135 instances for the uncoded articles, and it is the same error as moving the unit of analysis, because a count that assumes every record is full is a count of a different dataset from the one collected.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: compute chance-corrected agreement when coders use categories at different rates
questions.stem: Two coders each label one hundred extracts. They assign the same label on eighty-eight. Coder one calls seventy extracts present and coder two calls fifty-five. What is the chance-corrected agreement coefficient? Give the value to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Observed agreement is 0.88, and chance agreement from the two separate rates is 0.70 times 0.55 for both calling present plus 0.30 times 0.45 for both calling absent, which is 0.385 plus 0.135, or 0.52. Correcting gives 0.88 minus 0.52 over 0.48, which is 0.75, and the gap from the raw 0.88 is the part a careless reader would have credited to the coders when their two base rates differ so sharply.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.learningObjective: state what a saturation claim asserts about the code list and the sample
questions.stem: A paper reports that the team interviewed until no new themes appeared. What is that report actually claiming, and what is it not?

options.text: That new interviews stopped changing the code list, not that the findings hold everywhere or forever
That the sample was large enough to estimate the prevalence of each theme with a known margin
options.misconception: reads a stopping rule as though it were a precision guarantee for a proportion

options.text: That the code list is now final and no later interview could ever add a category to it
options.misconception: turns an observed plateau into a guarantee that no further data could change the analysis

options.text: That the team stopped as soon as the interviews became repetitive for the participants
options.misconception: confuses the researcher's sense of repetition with a change in the coded data

questions.explanation: A saturation claim is a bounded observation, that interviews added after a certain point stopped introducing new categories, which is evidence that the code list is adequate for this material and this team. It is not a sample-size calculation, a licence to treat the categories as permanently closed, or a claim that participants became repetitive, and the trap is that the word saturation sounds like a strong guarantee when in operation it is a modest claim about the analysis having stopped moving.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to keep happening for the claim to fail.

questions.topic: What a transferability claim rests on
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence a qualitative claim of transfer requires
questions.stem: A qualitative paper claims its finding travels to other settings. What does that claim have to rest on?

options.text: A description thick enough for a reader to judge whether the setting resembles their own
A large enough sample that the finding can be shown to be stable across many sites
options.misconception: imports the quantitative standard of sample size as the warrant for transfer

options.text: A published codebook, so any reader could re-run the same coding on their own data
options.misconception: treats a shared codebook as though it licensed a claim about other settings

options.text: A replication in a second country, without which no transfer may be discussed at all
options.misconception: requires a second full study before transfer can even be raised

questions.topic: What a member check establishes
questions.learningObjective: separate the accountability a member check provides from proof
questions.stem: A team circulates its themes to the participants, and three reply that the analysis misreads them. What has the member check established?

options.text: That participants can recognise and contest the account, which is an accountability to hold it to
That the analysis is correct, since the people studied are the final authority on their experience
options.misconception: treats a member check as a verdict that settles the analysis's truth

options.text: That the findings generalise, since several people's agreement establishes how common the finding is
options.misconception: converts agreement from a handful of people into a representativeness claim

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a reflexive record from a log of coding or fieldwork events

questions.topic: Sampling strategy in qualitative work
questions.learningObjective: judge a qualitative recruitment choice by its analytic purpose

Patients drawn at random from the full list, so every patient's chance of selection is equal

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why saturation-based sizing differs
questions.learningObjective: explain why a qualitative stopping rule is not a sample-size calculation
questions.stem: Why is a saturation-based sample not fixed in advance by a calculation the way an inferential sample is?

options.text: Because the stopping point is set by whether new interviews keep changing the code list
Because qualitative studies never produce a number, so no calculation could ever apply to them
options.misconception: denies that qualitative work produces counts at all, which is false

options.text: Because a calculation is only needed when the sample has to represent a wider population
options.misconception: claims the difference is about population representation rather than the stopping rule

options.text: Because interviews cost so little that a researcher can always afford to double the sample

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a qualitative finding does not generalise statistically
questions.learningObjective: explain the limit of a qualitative claim and what it must offer instead
questions.stem: A study of fourteen households reports that relatives do the booking whenever a discharge date changes. Explain why this cannot be stated as applying to all households, and what would be needed instead.

answer.exemplar: The fourteen households were not drawn to represent the population, so the finding establishes that this happens and how it works in the cases actually studied, and nothing in the design lets it carry the word all. Sampling error, the machinery that would let a small set speak for a large one, has no purchase here because the cases were chosen for what they could reveal rather than selected so that every household had a known chance of appearing. What the study can legitimately offer instead is a described mechanism, so that a reader can see the relatives taking over the booking, the decisions that shape it and the conditions under which it works, and can then judge for their own setting whether those conditions hold. That is transferability rather than statistical generalisation: the warrant is a description rich enough for someone else to recognise or reject the fit, not a margin of error attached to a proportion.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the cases were not chosen to represent a population, distinguishes transferability from statistical generalisation, and proposes a described mechanism thick enough for a reader to judge the fit themselves.
questions.hint: Ask how the fourteen households came to be the fourteen.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: How a grounded theory's categories emerge
questions.learningObjective: explain how categories can be shown to emerge from the material
questions.stem: A team says its study is grounded theory but published only its final category list. Explain why a final list alone cannot show the theory emerged from the data.

answer.exemplar: A final list of categories is consistent with a grounded analysis but equally consistent with a set decided in advance and used to sort the material, and the artefact that separates them is the revision, not the result. Constant comparison means an incoming interview or document is read against the existing categories, and any part of it that will not fit forces the category itself to change, so a grounded study can show an early code list that differs from the final one and can show what made the change necessary. Without that trail the reader cannot tell whether the categories answered the data or the data were read into the categories, and a cited framework, a large sample and a careful method section all fail to supply the missing evidence, because none of them records the analysis being unsettled by what it encountered. The test is whether the categories could have been written before the fieldwork; if they could, the claim that they emerged is not yet supported.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains constant comparison, says the revision trail is the evidence, and notes that a final list is equally consistent with categories fixed in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what the analysis would have had to do for the categories to change.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a reflexive record is not a field log
questions.learningObjective: explain what a reflexive record establishes and how it differs from a log
questions.stem: A researcher keeps a notebook of impressions, doubts and reactions alongside her interview notes. Explain what the impressions establish that the interview notes cannot, and why both are kept.

answer.exemplar: The interview notes record what was said and when, while the impressions record the researcher's own changing position, so the second is the only place where her assumptions, her rapport with particular participants and the moments she felt her questioning leading can be inspected. That matters because a qualitative analysis rests on an interpreter: the questions a researcher thinks to ask, the pauses they do not press, and the answers they recognise as significant are all filtered through a person, and none of that is visible in a transcript of the other side of the conversation. Keeping both means the evidence and the instrument that produced it are held together, so a reader can ask whether a theme tracks the participants' language or the researcher's interests, and so the researcher can notice mid-study that a set of interviews is going somewhere they had not planned. A dated log of events would supply none of this, because it would record that an interview took place without recording the person who was present at it.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates the record of what was said from the record of the researcher's own position, and says the second is what makes the interpretive work open to inspection.
questions.hint: Ask what the researcher's own reactions could do to the material.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why the two samples in a mixed study need not match
questions.learningObjective: explain why unequal phase samples are expected rather than a defect
questions.stem: A mixed study interviews thirty people in depth and then surveys two thousand others. Explain why the sizes should differ and what has to compensate for it.

answer.exemplar: The two phases are sized against different ends. The interviews are large enough for the code list to stop changing, which is a requirement about the analysis having converged, and going past that point adds interviews without adding knowledge. The survey is large enough for a proportion to carry a stated precision at a stated confidence, which is a requirement about estimation error and is essentially never satisfied by thirty cases. Because neither figure is the right size for the other's job, the mismatch is a symptom of a design working correctly rather than of an error, and pretending otherwise would mean either interviewing two thousand people or estimating a margin of error from thirty interviews. What compensates is the integration itself: a joint display in which each theme is set beside the quantitative result it bears on, so a reader can see which findings the larger sample supports, which it contradicts and which it simply does not reach, instead of the twenty-four or thirty carrying an authority that belongs to the survey and the survey appearing to speak for what the interviews found.

questions.explanation: A strong response says each phase is sized for a different requirement, so the mismatch is expected, and identifies the joint display as what has to do the work a shared sample would have done.
questions.hint: Ask what each sample had to be big enough to achieve.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a contradiction between convergent strands means
questions.learningObjective: explain why a convergent design can end in contradiction and how to read it
questions.stem: A convergent study finds that staff rate the new rota as fair while the survey shows sickness absence rising in the same unit. Explain why this contradiction is possible and what it should lead the team to do.

answer.exemplar: The two strands were built independently against their own questions, so nothing forced them to be measuring the same thing: the interviews asked what the rota feels like from the inside, and the survey asked whether people are well enough to be at work. A rota can be experienced as fair in the sense that the rules were explained properly and applied evenly, and still make the schedule harder to live with, so the two answers are not rivals but answers to two questions, and a convergent design is unusual in being able to show that at all. The right response is to put the two results together in a joint display and ask what each can and cannot speak to, which here means examining whether the absent are absent in the group the interviews covered. What must not happen is dropping the survey because interviews are easier to defend, recoding a variable until the numbers agree, or reporting the strand that reads better, since each of those removes the only evidence the design produced.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that independently built strands answer different questions, and calls for the contradiction to be examined in a joint display rather than resolved by discarding or recoding data.
questions.hint: Ask what each strand was built to measure before they met.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why the declared integration point is the test of a conclusion
questions.learningObjective: explain why a conclusion must be checked against the design's integration point
questions.stem: A design names a joint display as its integration point, and the paper's conclusion draws on both strands anyway. Explain why that conclusion still has to be checked against the integration point.

answer.exemplar: The integration point is where the design promised the strands would meet, so it fixes what kind of joint statement the study is in a position to make. If the display is the meeting place, then a conclusion has to be something the display supports: a finding both strands bear on, a divergence the display exposes, or a question the display shows is still open. When the display is missing, thin or only partly filled, the conclusion is resting on a combination nobody actually examined, and it becomes impossible to tell whether the two strands were weighed deliberately or simply placed in the same paragraph. This is what separates a mixed design from two studies printed together, and the check is cheap because the design was written down first and said exactly where the strands would meet. The trap is that a conclusion citing both sources looks integrated to a hurried reader, whereas the only thing that makes it integrated is that the declared meeting place exists and the conclusion can be traced into a row of it.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the integration point fixes which joint claims the design can support, and that a conclusion citing both strands is not integrated unless the declared meeting place exists and the claim traces into it.
questions.hint: Ask what the design said would be the place where the strands meet.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: From transcript to a named code
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that carry raw interview material into a coded extract
questions.stem: A team has a recorded interview and a codebook. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Fix and record the transcription convention, then produce the transcript
Read the transcript in full, then mark the passages that carry the code
Attach the code to each marked passage, recording its location
Check the marked passages against the codebook's boundary and examples
Log any passage the codebook cannot hold, for the next revision

questions.explanation: The transcript is the artefact everything else works on, so its conventions have to be settled and written down before anyone produces or reads it, or different parts of the study are coded against different renderings of the same words. The transcript is then read whole before anything is marked, because marking passage by passage turns the coder's attention forward and hides what the interview was doing before the first extract. Only then is the code attached with its location kept, so the decision is retrievable, and the codebook is consulted at that point to check the boundary really covers the passage rather than merely sounding close to it. Whatever the codebook cannot hold is logged rather than forced, because that record is the evidence that the scheme is answerable to the material and the input to its next revision.
questions.hint: Decide the rendering of the words before deciding what the words mean.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Running an explanatory sequential design
questions.learningObjective: sequence the phases of an explanatory sequential mixed design
questions.stem: A team has planned an explanatory sequential design. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Decide and record the point at which the two strands will be integrated
Run the survey and establish the result that now needs explaining
Design follow-up questions aimed at the mechanism behind that result
Run the follow-up interviews and code what participants say about it
Integrate the two, and let the explanation qualify the original result

questions.explanation: The integration point is fixed in the design, before anything is collected, because it determines what the second phase has to produce and therefore what questions should be asked of it. The survey then runs first and establishes the result, and only once that result is in hand can the team know what has to be explained, which is what makes the design explanatory rather than merely sequential. The follow-up questions are built to reach the mechanism behind the result, the interviews are run and coded, and the integration comes last and is allowed to qualify what the survey found, since a second strand that can only confirm the first would have been given no real job to do.
questions.hint: The design must say where the strands will meet before either one runs.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Running a focus group session
questions.learningObjective: sequence the preparation and conduct of a focus group session
questions.stem: A team is about to run its first focus group. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Order the guide from open to specific, and check the questions for order effects
Recruit a group that can discuss the topic together, rather than a convenience set
Agree who moderates, who facilitates, and how the recording will be made
Obtain consent and set ground rules before the discussion begins
Note who stayed quiet, and follow up with them individually afterwards

questions.explanation: The guide is designed and checked for order effects first, since an early sensitive item will shape everything after it and reordering a live session is not possible. Recruitment follows, because a group that cannot talk to each other produces nothing however well the guide runs, and the roles and the recording arrangement are settled before the day so that nobody has to negotiate them in front of participants. Consent and ground rules come at the start of the session itself, which is also where the discussion can be recorded without a participant objecting midway through. What the moderator cannot do is extract an answer from someone the format silences, so the quiet participants are noted and approached individually, which is how the group gives its account and the individual still gets to have theirs.
questions.hint: Design and staffing have to be settled before anybody walks into the room.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Deciding and reporting saturation
questions.learningObjective: sequence how a team reaches and justifies a stopping point
questions.stem: A team is deciding whether it has enough interviews. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Code each interview as it arrives, keeping the code list open to revision
Record how many new codes each new interview introduces
Keep interviewing while new codes are still appearing in the material
Continue a few interviews past the point where nothing new appears
Report the point reached, and bound the claim to this sample and code list

questions.explanation: Saturation is a property of the coding, so each interview has to be coded as it arrives against a code list that is still open, otherwise the count of new codes is an artefact of how closed the list already was. Those counts are then recorded interview by interview, and while new codes keep appearing the interviews must continue, because stopping at that moment reports a code list that the next interview would have changed. Interviewing a few cases past the plateau is what turns an apparent pause into evidence of one, and the report then gives the point reached together with its boundaries, because a saturation claim is a statement about this code list on this material and loses its force the moment it is written as though it were about the world.
questions.hint: The count of new codes only means something if the code list was still open.

questions.topic: Reading a mixed report with partial corroboration
questions.learningObjective: judge a mixed-methods report whose strands partly agree and partly conflict
questions.stem: A mixed study reports eight qualitative themes, of which three are confirmed by a survey result, two are contradicted by one, and three have no quantitative partner. What follows?

options.text: Integration happened and left conflicts, which need explaining rather than resolving by dropping a strand
The study is inconclusive, because a mixed design is only valid when both strands fully agree
options.misconception: treats complete agreement as the condition of a sound mixed design

options.text: The survey is the stronger evidence, so the three contradicted themes should not be reported
options.misconception: lets the strand with more cases overrule the other on disagreement alone

options.text: The design did not integrate, because three of the eight themes were never reached by the survey
options.misconception: treats a survey's silence about a theme as evidence of no integration

questions.explanation: Three confirmations and two contradictions are the display doing exactly the job it was built for, because a design that only ever produces agreement has told the reader nothing about which findings were robust, and the two conflicts are now visible as specific questions rather than as a general unease. questions.hint: Ask what the two contradicted rows are for.
